extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, judges, inventors, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and standards governing the required content, form, and sufficiency of a patent specification/description across classes of inventions (machine, art, combination, manufacture, composition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement — skilled person can construct and use
rubrics_metrics.description: If from the Description, taken in connection with its accompanying drawings and model, a person skilled in the art to which it belongs can by the exercise of his mechanical powers and information alone construct and use the invention, the ambiguity is not fatal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification must enable practice without requiring experimentation or inventive skill; sufficiency is judged by whether a competent skilled person can make and use the invention from the disclosure (cases referenced).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity fatality threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: If the inventor has left the invention 'wholly ambiguous and uncertain, so loosely defined, and so inaccurately expressed' that the court cannot, upon a fair interpretation of the words, gather what it is, the patent is void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will construe fairly and liberally; if fair interpretation reveals the nature and extent of the claim the patent may survive; ambiguity that prevents understanding by skilled persons is fatal. Ambiguity may sometimes be removed by considering oath or other application parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: False suggestion or concealment fatal
rubrics_metrics.description: A wilful false suggestion or concealment, in any point material to the invention or to the mode of making or using it, is fatal to the patent; the inventor must 'keep faith with the public'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wilful fraud is never presumed from mere defects but must be established by direct or circumstantial evidence; innocent omissions or imperfections that can be otherwise explained are not presumed fraudulent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form of Description is flexible but must be clear
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject to substantive rules, the Description is left to the judgment and choice of the inventor; no particular form of words is prescribed, though the clearest and most easily understood expressions should be selected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventor may use concrete illustrations or enumerate properties; choose the clearest phrasing when alternatives exist; a choice of expressions should select the clearest option (Ex parte Gould).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify the art at the outset
rubrics_metrics.description: At the outset the Description ought to specify the particular art to which the invention appertains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stating the field helps readers understand the invention and interpret the description correctly; it's good practice to situate the invention before details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish old from new; rely on Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The old and the new may be distinguished by separate delineations, or both may be embraced in one general Description and the line subsequently drawn between them by the Claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When describing prior patented subject-matter, the prior patent may be referred to and incorporated; the patentee is bound by the description he gives when distinguishing new from old.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation vs requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Words of recommendation are different from a requirement; a recommendation is optional, while a requirement (a necessity) is essential to practise the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omitting a recommendation (a suggested method) will not be fatal if the invention can be accomplished by other means; omitting something known to be necessary to enjoyment of the invention is fatal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe means or result with mode of obtaining it
rubrics_metrics.description: The application of a new natural force or principle may be described either by describing the result with the mode of obtaining it, or by describing the means employed to produce the result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General words describing an effect do not describe the cause unless cause and effect are indissolubly connected; describing the means that necessarily produce the result is sufficient even if the inventor does not state the abstract principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect/abstract description limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: General words describing an effect do not describe the cause unless the cause and the effect are indissolubly connected and are commensurate with each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An inventor need not understand the abstract principle, but must describe the new and useful application sufficiently; if the cause does not invariably produce the effect, more concrete disclosure is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic specification may describe one species
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification for a generic invention need describe but one species, though it may describe more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describing a representative species can be sufficient for a generic claim, but the description must enable the claimed scope; constructions illustrating generic claims may be described even if they are not themselves claimed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class-of-substances rule
rubrics_metrics.description: The description of a class of substances as an element in the invention is not correct except when each substance in the class will serve the purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If any substance in the claimed class will not answer the purpose, the patent is void as to that generic formulation (see Schneider v. Thill).

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination inventions — elements and co-operative law
rubrics_metrics.description: The essential features of a combination are its several elements and their co-operative law; each must be specifically described and the drawings as well as the written matter must represent the elements in combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requirement applies even where elements are old and well known; parts that are useless or merely incidental may be omitted unless needed to render the new combination intelligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe old elements and mode of combining
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification of a combination of old elements must describe the old elements and the mode of combining them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where elements of a combination are clearly pointed out other particulars of construction may be unnecessary; the patentee's description binds him when he limits equivalents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art inventions — acts and means must be described
rubrics_metrics.description: The essential characteristics of an art reside in the acts of which it is composed; these acts must be correctly, completely, and intelligibly described. Physical means and the mode of using them must also be particularly delineated unless obvious to those skilled in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Description need not include every physical means by which the art may be exercised, provided the art can be successfully practised by using the apparatus actually described according to the rule laid down.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine inventions — structural law and essential parts
rubrics_metrics.description: A machine's essence is its structural law, which must be correctly and intelligibly explained. The best mode of constructing and employing the mechanism must be described; every integral part with its position, relation, and essential details of shape, proportion, and materials should be delineated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Known mechanical elements (wedges, pulleys, etc.) need not be described in detail; dimensions, velocities, and routine adjustments ordinarily known to mechanics can be left to the constructor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacture inventions — essential qualities or process
rubrics_metrics.description: A manufacture's essential qualities (those without which it would cease to be the particular invention) should be enumerated, or, if not possible, the process by which the manufacture is produced may be particularly delineated to define the product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The manufacture must be fully explained and distinguished from other inventions; when the manufacture can be understood without describing the producing process or machine, those need not be mentioned and defects in their description do not vitiate the manufacture's description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition inventions — ingredients, mixing, result
rubrics_metrics.description: A composition of matter requires description of the ingredients, their mode of intermixture, and the resulting composition. Each ingredient must be completely and exactly described; nothing must be left to experiment as to their nature or number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No substance should be specified as an ingredient unless essential; the inventor is bound by the ingredients he specifies and cannot later claim compositions lacking those essential elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excessive description non-fatal unless fraudulent
rubrics_metrics.description: An excess of description does not injure the patent, unless the addition be fraudulent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extra illustrative matter is permissible; only additions intended to mislead or conceal material facts will be held fatal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity may be resolved by other application parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Any ambiguity in the Description may be removed by the oath or other parts of the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may look to the whole application (oath, drawings, models) to construe ambiguous passages; however, if the Description has no apparent meaning when construed, the patent is void.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description must enable without further inventive skill
rubrics_metrics.description: The Description must so disclose the invention that no further exercise of inventive skill is necessary in order to practise it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If practice of the invention requires further invention or material experimentation by the public, the Description is insufficient (cases: Neilson v. Harford, Morgan v. Seaward and others cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mode of use is not description of the thing used
rubrics_metrics.description: A device is not portrayed by the delineation of its mode of use, nor is the use itself described unless a practical rule is given by following which the desired result can be obtained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describing only the manner of using an article without describing the article itself is insufficient; to claim a use, the specification must provide a practical rule enabling the use.
